scenes.title: What does it mean to own a bitcoin?
scenes.narration: What does it mean to own a bitcoin?

scenes.title: Friends keep one list of who paid whom
scenes.narration: Start with something simpler. A few friends pay for each other’s dinners, and they keep one shared list of who paid whom.

steps.say: Alice pays Bob twenty dollars, so she writes it down.
More lines go on the list as the month goes by.
At the end of the month they settle up. Whoever is down puts cash in a pot, and whoever is up takes cash out.
But anyone can add a line. What stops Bob from writing that Alice pays him a hundred dollars?

scenes.narration: The fix is a digital signature.

steps.say: Each person makes a pair of keys: a secret key they never share, and a public key everyone can see.
Alice runs her line and her secret key through a signing function.
Out comes a signature, a string of five hundred and twelve bits.
Anyone can check that signature against the line and Alice’s public key. The answer is true.
If Bob changes the line, the old signature no longer fits, and the check says false.
Without Alice’s secret key, he cannot make a new one.

scenes.narration: Here are real signatures made with one secret key. Watch what happens when the line changes.

steps.say: This is Alice’s signature for paying Bob a hundred dollars.
Change one character, a hundred to a hundred and one, and the signature looks completely different.
Put the old one on a changed line, and the check fails.
But Bob can still copy the whole signed line, word for word.
The copy checks out, so Alice would pay him twice.
So every line gets a number of its own, and signing covers that number too.
Now a repeat has a number that is already on the list, and everyone ignores it.

scenes.narration: Signatures stop fake lines, but not debt.

steps.say: Charlie could run up a huge bill and vanish.
So add a rule: everyone starts with a hundred.
And a line counts only if the list shows the payer has the money.
Charlie pays Alice sixty. He can cover it, so the line counts, and he has forty left.
Charlie pays Bob forty. That leaves him with nothing.
Alice pays David twenty. She has plenty.
Then Charlie tries to pay David thirty. Read the list from the top, and he has nothing left.
So everyone rejects that line.
Notice that nobody holds any dollars now. The money is just the list, so call it ledger dollars.
Owning some means the history says you have them.

steps.say: So drop the website. Instead, everyone keeps their own copy of the list.
To pay Bob, Alice broadcasts her signed line to everyone, and each person adds it to their copy.
But messages take time to travel. At the same moment, David sends a line of his own.
Charlie and David get his line first, so their copies have the other order.
Now the copies disagree. With no one in charge, how does everyone agree on one history?

draw.write: two orders, no one in charge

scenes.narration: The answer needs one more tool, a hash function called SHA-256.

steps.say: It takes any text, short or long. Here, Hello, with a capital H.
It gives back two hundred and fifty six bits, written here as sixty four hex digits.
Change just that one letter to lower case, and the whole result changes.
Nothing about it is close to the first.
And there is no way back.
To find text with a given hash, all you can do is guess, and the guesses would outlast the universe.

steps.say: Take a batch of lines, add a number called a nonce, and hash the lot.
The goal is a hash that starts with thirty zero bits.
With a nonce of zero, the hash starts with only 1 zero bit.
So try one, then two, then three. Each guess gives a hash that looks random.
Our computer kept going for a few minutes, and this number finally worked.
Each bit halves the odds, so thirty zeros takes about two to the thirty guesses, around a billion.
Finding it is slow, but checking it is fast. Anyone can hash the lines with this nonce once and see the zeros.

scenes.title: Each block holds the hash of the one before

steps.say: A block counts only if it solves the puzzle. Block one’s hash starts with the zeros its nonce bought.
Block two writes that hash at its top.
So does every block after, about the one before it. That links them into a chain.
Now say someone changes an old line in block one, ten to a hundred. Its hash changes completely, and no longer starts with zeros.
Block two still points at the old hash, so the link is broken, and everyone can see it.
To hide the change, the cheat must solve the puzzle again for block one, then for every block after it.

scenes.narration: People called miners collect the lines everyone broadcasts and race to solve the puzzle for the next block.

steps.say: Maya solves it first. The first line of her block pays her ten ledger dollars out of thin air.
That reward is the only way new money appears.
But Omar solved a different block four at nearly the same moment. Now there are two chains of the same length.
The next miner happens to build on Maya’s block. That chain is longer now, and everyone follows the longest chain.
Omar’s block is dropped, and its lines go back into the pool.

steps.say: Alice pays Bob in one block.
Meanwhile she secretly builds another chain, where that payment never happened.
If her chain gets longer, everyone switches to it, and her money comes back.
But her one machine races everyone else’s together. Say she has a tenth of all the computing power.
If Bob waits for one block on top of his payment, her chance of ever catching up is about one in five.
Each extra block makes it much smaller. After six blocks it is about two in ten thousand.
So Bob waits a few blocks before he trusts the payment.

steps.say: The network adjusts the puzzle every two thousand and sixteen blocks, about two weeks, so a new block comes about every ten minutes.
In two thousand and nine, each block paid its miner fifty bitcoin.
Every two hundred and ten thousand blocks, about four years, the reward halves.
Twenty five, then twelve and a half, then six and a quarter.
Since twenty twenty four it is three point one two five.
Add up every halving and the total stops just short of twenty one million bitcoin.
Blocks also have a size limit, so people add a small fee for a spot, and miners pick the lines that pay best.
As the reward shrinks, fees pay more of the miners’ bills.

scenes.narration: Each problem we hit along the way got one tool.

steps.say: Signatures and IDs stop fake and copied lines.
The shared history decides who owns what.
And proof of work, with the longest chain, lets strangers agree on one history without anyone in charge.
